report:
## Conclusion

**The claim is well-supported by the evidence.** Multiple studies and meta-analyses consistently show that bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with significantly greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared to receiving no bystander CPR.

### Key Evidence:

1. **Swedish nationwide study (Circulation, 2019):** In a study of 30,445 OHCA patients over 18 years, any form of bystander CPR—including compression-only CPR—was associated with nearly **2-fold higher survival** compared to no bystander CPR. As compression-only CPR adoption increased six-fold, overall survival improved. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30929457/); [AHA Circulation](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.038179))

2. **AHA Science Advisory (2008):** The American Heart Association concluded that adult victims of OHCA who receive bystander hands-only CPR or conventional CPR have a similar chance of survival—both clearly superior to no intervention. ([AHA Journals](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380))

3. **Meta-analysis (The Lancet, 2010):** Dispatcher-assisted chest-compression-only bystander CPR was associated with improved survival after OHCA compared with standard CPR, and both forms outperformed no CPR. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673610614547))

4. **Narrative review (2024):** Confirmed that "any type of CPR is associated with double survival when compared to not receiving CPR before emergency medical service arrival." ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S110996662400201X))

### Summary

The evidence strongly supports the claim. Bystander hands-only CPR roughly doubles survival compared to no bystander CPR, and it performs at least as well as conventional CPR with rescue breaths for adult primary cardiac arrest. This underpins current AHA guidelines recommending hands-only CPR for lay bystanders.
